title: Build a transformer from scratch
summary: Implement every block of a tiny transformer in numpy + train it on a toy task — an 8-week capstone.
contentIntro:
## What you'll build

A tiny transformer — small enough to train on your laptop, complete enough to teach you how every block works. Six milestones: tokenizer, attention, multi-head, the full block, training, sampling.

No magic libraries. Numpy + a little PyTorch where it makes the writeup clearer. By the end, you'll have a runnable model + a portfolio page that proves you can build one.

[[attention]] is the wedge — once you can derive scaled dot-product attention, the rest of the architecture clicks into place.
contentUndergrad:
## What you'll build

A 2-layer transformer that learns a copy task. You'll author every primitive — BPE tokenizer, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, FFN + residual + layer norm, training loop, sampling — in a working notebook + writeup combination.

## Format

Six milestones, ~10-14 days each. Each milestone has:

- A **runnable test harness** (Pyodide-executable assertions on your code)
- A **rubric** the AI grader uses to score correctness, derivation rigor, and writeup depth
- An optional **lab** for the conceptual piece (e.g. a heatmap that updates as you tweak Q/K/V)

When all six pass, your public artifact page goes live at `/capstones/c/${username}-transformer-from-scratch` — share it as portfolio.

## Why this capstone

Reading attention papers gives you a feel; building it gives you the mechanism. The grader doesn't care about your hyperparameters — it cares whether your writeup demonstrates you can derive √d_k scaling, explain residuals, and notice when training diverges.

[[attention]] · [[softmax]]
contentGrad:
## What you'll build

A from-scratch transformer rebuilt around the small-model regime: enough parameters to verify scaling laws don't dominate, simple enough to ablate every architectural choice. The defense (claim-thread Q&A on the artifact page) is part of the rubric — be ready to argue why scaled dot-product attention beats additive, why pre-norm beats post-norm in the regime you trained, and what your training curve says about the underlying optimization landscape.

[[attention]] is necessary but not sufficient. Reviewers will probe your understanding of induction heads, your ablations on head count, and the empirical behavior of your loss curve.

milestones.title: Tokens & embeddings
milestones.description:
Implement a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer + embedding lookup table.

- Start with character-level vocab
- Merge the most frequent adjacent pair, repeat for N merges
- Embed each token to a `d_model`-dimensional vector
- Show the token-count drop curve as you increase merges

:::lab[tokenizer-playground-lab]

In your writeup: explain why subword tokens beat both characters and whitespace tokens for English. Include a diagram or chart from your tokenizer in action.

criteria.description: Tokenizer produces correct merges + embedding lookup is correct.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the artifacts (GitHub / writeup) demonstrate a correct BPE merge loop + a working embedding lookup.
Score the depth of the writeup's argument for subword tokenization vs character / whitespace alternatives.

criteria.description: Demonstrated the tokenizer with a chart.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the submission includes a chart or diagram showing the tokenizer in action (token count curve, merge progression, etc.).

milestones.title: Scaled dot-product attention
milestones.description:
Implement `attention(Q, K, V)` from scratch in numpy. The math:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

:::lab[attention-weights-lab]

Visualize the attention weights on a 6-token sequence. In your writeup: derive the √d_k scaling factor + explain why it matters. Show what happens to the softmax when you remove it (gradient saturation).

criteria.aiPrompt: Score correctness of the scaled dot-product attention implementation including the √d_k scaling.
Score the rigor of the writeup's derivation of why √d_k scaling is needed (variance of dot products, softmax saturation).
Score whether the submission visualizes attention weights on a concrete sequence.

milestones.title: Multi-head attention
milestones.description:
Extend single-head attention to multi-head:

- Split `d_model` into `n_heads × d_head`
- Run attention independently per head
- Concatenate + linear-project back to `d_model`

Ablate `n_heads` ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}. Plot training loss vs head count on the toy copy task.

In your writeup: explain why multi-head helps. (Hint: it's not parameter count.)

criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether MHA correctly splits the d_model dimension into heads, runs attention per head, and concatenates back.

criteria.description: Ran an ablation on head count.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the submission includes an ablation on n_heads + an interpretation of the result.
Score the writeup's argument for why multi-head attention helps beyond a single big head.

milestones.title: FFN + residual + layer norm
milestones.description:
Build the rest of the transformer block:

- Position-wise feedforward (linear → GELU → linear)
- Residual connections around each sub-layer
- Layer norm (pre- or post-norm — your choice; defend it in the writeup)

Visualize gradient flow through the block during training. Show what happens when you remove the residual.

In your writeup: explain the role of residual connections + why layer norm beats batch norm here.

criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the submission's full transformer block (FFN + residual + LN) is correctly assembled.
Score whether the submission visualizes or analyzes gradient flow through the block.

criteria.description: Defends pre/post norm + LN vs BN.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score the writeup's argument for the chosen norm placement + LN vs BN.

milestones.title: Train on a toy task
milestones.description:
Train your 2-layer transformer on a toy copy task: input is a sequence of N random tokens, target is the same sequence reversed (or copied — your choice).

- Hold-out a validation set
- Plot training + val loss curves
- Show 5+ sample outputs from the trained model

In your writeup: tell the training story. What surprised you? Did you have to tune learning rate, batch size, sequence length? What does the loss curve say?

criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the model demonstrates convergence on the toy task (val loss drops, sample outputs are reasonable).
Score whether the included sample outputs demonstrate the model has learned the task.
Score whether the writeup tells a real story about training (what was tried, what failed, what was learned).

milestones.title: Sample + reflect
milestones.description:
Implement greedy + temperature sampling. Show side-by-side outputs at temperatures {0.1, 0.7, 1.5}.

:::lab[sampling-temperature-lab]

Final reflection: what did this capstone teach you that reading papers couldn't? What would you do differently? Where do you think your model fails — and why?

criteria.aiPrompt: Score correctness of greedy + temperature sampling implementations.
Score whether the submission includes a meaningful comparison across temperatures.
Score the depth of the final reflection. Reward concrete, honest observations about what was learned and where the model fails. Penalise generic 'I learned a lot' filler.
